name: Cipactli
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Cipactli is more than a simple zoological “crocodile.” In central Mexican visual culture it can evoke a primordial aquatic-earth creature, sometimes combining traits of crocodilians, serpents, and sawfish. Archaeological and iconographic studies emphasize that the being is deliberately composite rather than a naturalistic species.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: In creation accounts, Cipactli can evoke the animate being from whose body the ordered earth was formed [S8]. Its earth-making role connects it with the basis of life and growth; its emergence from primordial waters links earth with watery origins. As the first sign, it can also evoke beginnings [S1, S2].
cultural_and_historical_context:
In several sixteenth-century Nahua creation accounts, the first earth is formed from a monstrous being dwelling in the primordial waters. One version describes the gods making the earth from Cipactli. Other accounts closely associate this earth-being with Tlaltecuhtli, the animate, consuming earth. Diana Magaloni Kerpel describes the mythic creature as a monstrous “lagarto” floating in the primeval waters whose body becomes the ordered world.

This gives Cipactli a strong association with beginnings, the emergence of land, generative earth, and the dangerous living foundation of creation. It is significant that Cipactli stands first in the twenty-sign sequence.

Sahagún begins his detailed account of the tonalpohualli with the trecena Ce Cipactli (1 Cipactli). That trecena is described as favorable in Book IV, but this does not mean every Cipactli day was automatically “lucky.” The numeral and place within the trecena matter.
app_safe_description: Cipactli is the first sign of the twenty-day sequence. Its crocodilian form recalls the primordial earth-creature of central Mexican creation traditions—the living being from which the ordered earth was formed. The sign therefore carries a strong connection to beginnings, earth, generation, and the powerful forces beneath the human world.

name: Ehecatl
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Ehēcatl means wind. In central Mexican religion, wind was not merely weather: it was an active force that moved clouds, announced rain, swept and opened space, and set cosmic processes into motion.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: Ehecatl evokes an invisible force that moves through and changes the world [S2, S4]. Wind can suggest breath, clearing, the movement of clouds and rain, and cosmic motion in Ehecatl-Quetzalcoatl traditions [S1, S2]. Breath is a broader association, not the glyph’s literal meaning.
cultural_and_historical_context:
The divine form Ehecatl-Quetzalcoatl was closely associated with wind. The wind god’s projecting mask or beak is among the most distinctive iconographic features in central Mexican art. In creation traditions, Quetzalcoatl also participates in setting the present world in motion and in bringing life to humanity.

Wind therefore evokes movement, breath, invisible force, and the opening of pathways. These are broader cultural associations, not a fixed horoscope definition.
app_safe_description: Ehecatl means “Wind.” Its imagery is connected with Ehecatl-Quetzalcoatl and with wind as an invisible force that moves through the world, clears paths, carries clouds, and participates in cosmic motion.

name: Calli
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Calli literally means house. The glyph represents built, inhabited space: a place enclosed from the outside world.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: The house marks protected, inhabited space. It can evoke household continuity, family, inheritance, domestic ritual, work, production, and the household as a basic social unit. Calli also participates in naming years as one of four year-bearer signs [S2, S6].
cultural_and_historical_context:
For Nahua communities the house was not merely a private residence. It was a fundamental social unit tied to family, household ritual, inheritance, production, lineage, and community organization. House imagery therefore marks the human-made and inhabited world.

Calli is especially important because it is one of the four year-bearer signs used in naming the 52 years of the calendrical cycle, along with Tochtli, Acatl, and Tecpatl.
app_safe_description: Calli means “House.” It represents the built and inhabited world—the household as a place of family, continuity, work, ritual, and social life. Calli is also one of the four signs used as a bearer of year names in the 52-year cycle.

name: Cuetzpalin
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Cuetzpalin is the lizard. The historical sources sometimes explain auguries by referring directly to observed animal behavior.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: Sahagún’s 1-Lizard passage compares bodily toughness and recovery with a lizard surviving a fall and quickly running away [S1]. This specific trecena interpretation draws on animal observation; it should not be generalized into a fixed meaning for every Cuetzpalin day.
cultural_and_historical_context:
Sahagún’s discussion of the trecena Ce Cuetzpalin (1 Lizard) says that people born in that sign were compared to the lizard’s physical toughness: a lizard could fall and immediately run away unharmed. The text associates the trecena with bodily vigor, diligence, and work.

This is a good example of how Nahua divination could draw meaning from observation and analogy with the natural world.

Those passages describe Ce Cuetzpalin and its trecena, not a universal personality definition for every date containing the Cuetzpalin glyph.
app_safe_description: Cuetzpalin means “Lizard.” Sahagún preserves an interpretation of the 1-Lizard trecena that compares human vigor and resilience with the lizard’s ability to survive falls and quickly continue moving. The sign shows how animal behavior could become part of calendrical symbolism.

name: Coatl
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Coatl means serpent. Serpents appear throughout Mesoamerican religious imagery and could connect earth, water, fertility, sky, rulership, and supernatural power depending on context.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: Serpents belong to a widespread sacred visual vocabulary [S2]. Depending on context they can connect earth, water, fertility, sky, rulership, or divine force. Quetzalcoatl’s feathered-serpent image joins serpent and precious-feather imagery, but does not define every serpent. In the Caso correlation, 1-Coatl is the anchor associated with August 13, 1521 Julian [S6].
cultural_and_historical_context:
It would be wrong to reduce every serpent image to one concept. Quetzalcoatl (“Feathered Serpent”) combines serpent and precious-feather imagery, while other serpentine beings belong to different environmental and divine complexes.

For the day sign, the safest approach is to retain the serpent as a powerful living category of sacred imagery rather than assign one personality trait.

Coatl is especially important for this app because the Alfonso Caso correlation commonly uses 1-Coatl as the tonalpohualli date corresponding to 13 August 1521 (Julian), the fall of Tenochtitlan.
app_safe_description: Coatl means “Serpent.” Serpents were among the most important visual beings in Mesoamerican religion, appearing in imagery related to earth, water, fertility, celestial forces, and divine power. The day sign belongs to that broad sacred visual world rather than to one fixed character type.

name: Miquiztli
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Miquiztli means death. Its glyph usually uses unmistakable skeletal imagery.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: The skull glyph names death directly. Nahua sources describe differentiated postmortem destinations; in broader religious contexts, death, sacrifice, decomposition, and fertility could be intertwined. Sahagún describes 1-Miquiztli as mixed, while Durán gives a darker account [S1, S7], cautioning against a universal “bad luck” gloss.
cultural_and_historical_context:
In Nahua thought, death was not simply the abstract opposite of life. Different forms of death were tied to different postmortem destinations and ritual meanings. Death imagery belonged to a larger cosmic system in which decomposition, sacrifice, fertility, and renewal could be closely connected.

The historical sources warn us against assuming that a sign named “Death” was automatically evil. Sahagún describes Ce Miquiztli (1 Death) as mixed—having favorable and unfavorable positions—and says devotion and ritual conduct mattered. Durán gives a darker assessment. The disagreement itself is evidence that the tradition should not be flattened into one modern keyword.
app_safe_description: Miquiztli means “Death” and is represented by a skull. Although its name can sound ominous to a modern reader, sixteenth-century sources do not give it one simple meaning: Sahagún and Durán preserve different assessments, and the fortune of a date depended on its full calendrical setting.

name: Mazatl
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Mazatl means deer. Deer were economically and ritually important animals across Mesoamerica, associated with hunting, wilderness, meat, hides, bone, and offerings.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: Deer evoke the landscape beyond cultivation and relationships involving hunting and subsistence. They provided meat and useful materials and also appear in ritual and visual traditions [S2, S3]. The sign brings this consequential animal into sacred time.
cultural_and_historical_context:
The deer belongs strongly to the hunted landscape beyond cultivated settlement. In Mesoamerican imagery more broadly, deer appear in hunting and sacrificial contexts and as calendrical beings.

The day sign therefore draws on a real ecological and ritual relationship, not merely an abstract emblem.
app_safe_description: Mazatl means “Deer.” Deer were important animals in Mesoamerican hunting, subsistence, ritual, and imagery. As a day sign, Mazatl brings the animal of the hunted landscape into the sacred count of time.

name: Tochtli
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Tochtli means rabbit.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: Rabbit reproduction can evoke fertility and abundance, but this is an interpretive association, not a universal divinatory verdict. Tochtli is closely linked with the maguey/pulque complex and the Centzon Totochtin (“Four Hundred Rabbits”) [S1, S2, S7]. Pulque had ceremonial and social roles. “Cyclical excess” is a cautious synthesis of varied intoxication associations, not a literal translation. Tochtli is also a year-bearer [S2, S6].
cultural_and_historical_context:
Rabbit imagery has a rich relationship with the maguey/pulque complex. The divine beings known collectively as the Centzon Totochtin (“Four Hundred Rabbits”) personified the many forms or effects of pulque intoxication. The calendrical name Ome Tochtli (2 Rabbit) became especially important in this context.

That does not mean every Tochtli day means “drunkenness.” Rabbit imagery also belongs to wider themes of ritual feasting, fertility, maguey, and specific divine complexes.

Tochtli is also one of the four year-bearer signs.
app_safe_description: Tochtli means “Rabbit.” Rabbit imagery was closely connected with the maguey-and-pulque religious complex, including the many rabbit deities called the Centzon Totochtin. Tochtli is also one of the four signs used to name years in the 52-year cycle.

name: Atl
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Atl means water, one of the central substances of Nahua cosmology and daily survival.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: Water sustains life and agriculture, linking the sign with rain, crops, lakes, and urban life in the Basin of Mexico. Springs, rivers, lakes, and rain belong to overlapping sacred and environmental relationships [S2, S3]. Water nourishes but can also flood and exceed human control.
cultural_and_historical_context:
Rain, springs, lakes, rivers, irrigation, agriculture, mountains, and fertility formed overlapping sacred relationships. Tlaloc and Chalchiuhtlicue are among the best-known water-associated deities, but water symbolism extends far beyond one god.

Tenochtitlan itself existed within an intensely managed lacustrine environment. Water was therefore simultaneously life-giving, agricultural, urban, dangerous, and sacred.
app_safe_description: Atl means “Water.” Its glyph represents the substance essential to rain, agriculture, lakes, springs, and life in the Basin of Mexico. Water could nourish and sustain, but it also belonged to powerful divine and environmental forces beyond human control.

name: Itzcuintli
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Itzcuintli means dog.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: Dogs were familiar household animals and also had mortuary associations. Central Mexican sources describe dogs helping the dead journey toward Mictlan [S1, S2], connecting the sign with passage between the living world and the realm of the dead without making the animal inherently negative.
cultural_and_historical_context:
Dogs had practical roles in Mesoamerican households, but they also carried strong mortuary associations. Colonial and archaeological sources describe dogs as beings capable of assisting the dead in the difficult journey through the underworld, especially in relation to crossing water on the path toward Mictlan.

This helps explain why dog symbolism can sit naturally beside the death-and-underworld complex without making the animal itself “negative.”
app_safe_description: Itzcuintli means “Dog.” Beyond their everyday role, dogs had important mortuary associations in central Mexico and could be imagined as helpers of the dead on the journey toward Mictlan. The day sign therefore belongs to both the familiar human household and the sacred geography of death.

name: Ozomahtli
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Ozomahtli means monkey.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: Monkey imagery is associated with music, dance, and performance [S1, S2]. The Xochipilli association places it near artistic activity, though patron mappings vary by tradition. Sahagún’s 1-Monkey account includes singing and sociability, and also connects the trecena with the Cihuateteo. Joyful and dangerous associations coexist; this is not a universal personality profile.
cultural_and_historical_context:
Monkey imagery became closely associated with music, dance, performance, pleasure, and artistic activity. This connection appears in several central Mexican sources and fits the broader religious sphere of Xochipilli/Macuilxochitl.

Sahagún’s discussion of Ce Ozomahtli (1 Monkey) describes people born under that trecena in terms that include sociability and singing. It also records a more ominous dimension: the trecena was associated with the descent of the Cihuateteo, dangerous spirits connected with women who died in childbirth, and families protected young children from them.

That combination is important: a single trecena could carry both celebratory and dangerous sacred qualities.
app_safe_description: Ozomahtli means “Monkey.” In central Mexican religious imagery the monkey was strongly associated with music, dance, artistry, and performance. Sahagún’s account of the 1-Monkey trecena also connects it with the dangerous Cihuateteo, showing that calendrical symbolism could contain joyful and threatening forces at the same time.

name: Malinalli
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Malinalli refers to grass, often represented in a twisted or bundled form. The visual form matters because grasses and fibers were useful materials woven, twisted, tied, and transformed.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: Malinalli evokes grass in cultivated and uncultivated landscapes. Plant fibers could be twisted, tied, woven, and made useful; the bundled glyph may suggest prepared material. Some patron tables connect it with Patecatl and medicinal/pulque associations [S2, S3]. “Transformation” is an interpretation, not the lexical meaning.
cultural_and_historical_context:
Grass belongs to the cultivated and uncultivated landscape and to everyday technologies such as rope, mats, bindings, and woven material. Boone notes that the day-sign vocabulary includes plants and natural substances that would have been immediately recognizable in ordinary life.

The common patron association with Patecatl also links Malinalli in some calendrical tables with the medicinal and pulque complex.
app_safe_description: Malinalli is usually translated as “Grass” and is often shown as a twisted or bundled plant. Its image draws from the ordinary plant materials that surrounded Nahua life and could be cut, woven, bound, and transformed into useful objects.

name: Acatl
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Acatl means reed.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: Reeds belonged to central Mexico’s wetland ecology and supplied materials for construction, mats, and other technologies. Acatl is one of four year-bearers [S2, S6]. Ce Acatl appears in traditions concerning Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl, though later narratives vary and require care.
cultural_and_historical_context:
Reeds were common plants in the lacustrine environment of central Mexico and were used in construction, mats, tools, and other everyday technologies. “Reed” also occurs in major calendrical names and mytho-historical dates.

The year Ce Acatl (1 Reed) is famous because colonial traditions link it with Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl, though later historical narratives about these dates must be handled cautiously.

Acatl is one of the four year bearers.
app_safe_description: Acatl means “Reed.” Reeds belonged to the lake environment and everyday material life of central Mexico, but Acatl also carried major calendrical importance as one of the four signs used to name years. Certain Reed years became prominent in later historical and sacred narratives.

name: Ocelotl
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Ocelotl denotes the jaguar or a powerful spotted feline.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: The jaguar’s predatory strength informs its visual charge. Its nocturnal habits can evoke night, caves, and underworld settings; jaguar imagery also appears in royal and martial contexts and can carry sacred force [S2]. Sahagún’s unfavorable account concerns the 1-Ocelotl trecena, not every Ocelotl day [S1].
cultural_and_historical_context:
The jaguar was one of the most charged animals in Mesoamerican visual culture. Its nocturnal habits, strength, predatory power, and ability to move through dense landscape made it an important image of night, earth, caves, rulership, warfare, and supernatural force in different contexts.

The Mexica elite military identity commonly called the “jaguar warrior” shows one martial use of feline imagery, although the calendar sign should not be reduced to warfare.
app_safe_description: Ocelotl means “Jaguar.” The jaguar was a major symbol of predatory strength and nocturnal power throughout Mesoamerica and appears in royal, martial, underworld, and sacred imagery. In the tonalpohualli, however, its exact augury depended on the numbered day and trecena rather than on the feline image alone.

name: Cuauhtli
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Cuauhtli means eagle.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: The eagle’s flight evokes sky and height, while central Mexican traditions connect eagle imagery with solar force, warfare, sacrifice, and political authority [S2, S3]. The eagle is central to the Mexica foundation narrative of Tenochtitlan, one strand of the sign’s broader history.
cultural_and_historical_context:
The eagle was deeply tied to the sun, height, warfare, sacrifice, and elite power. The Mexica foundation narrative of Tenochtitlan famously centers on the eagle appearing on the cactus, and eagle imagery also formed part of elite military identity.

Yet the eagle was not only a political emblem. Its flight and relation to the sky made it a natural vehicle for solar and celestial symbolism.
app_safe_description: Cuauhtli means “Eagle.” Eagles were associated with the sky, solar force, warfare, sacrifice, and political power in central Mexican imagery. The eagle also became central to the Mexica account of the founding of Tenochtitlan.

name: Cozcacuauhtli
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Cozcacuauhtli refers to a vulture, frequently identified iconographically with a king-vulture-like bird.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: As a scavenger, the vulture is ecologically linked with carrion; renewal through consumption is an interpretive observation, not a fixed ancient gloss. Sahagún connects the 1-Vulture trecena with elders and long life while noting that not all share that fate [S1].
cultural_and_historical_context: Vultures transform carrion into life for themselves and occupy a boundary between death, decay, sky, and renewal. That ecological reality made the bird visually distinctive, although we should not assume one universal symbolic definition.
app_safe_description: Cozcacuauhtli means “Vulture.” Sahagún describes the 1-Vulture trecena as associated with elders, prosperity, and long life, while explicitly noting that not every person born within it would share the same destiny. The passage is a useful reminder that Nahua divination was not mechanically deterministic.

name: Ollin
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Ollin means movement. It should not automatically be translated as “earthquake,” although earthquakes can be one manifestation of movement.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: Ollin means movement and names dynamic change. Nahui Ollin (“4 Movement”) names the present cosmic era; the Sun Stone’s program associates the sign with the four preceding eras and a dynamic cosmos [S2]. Earthquake can be one manifestation, but does not exhaust its meaning.
app_safe_description: Ollin means “Movement.” The sign is especially important because the present cosmic era was known as Nahui Ollin, “4 Movement.” On monuments such as the Sun Stone, Ollin expresses the dynamic and changing condition of the cosmos rather than merely an earthquake.

name: Tecpatl
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Técpatl means flint, especially the sharp stone blade.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: Flint was shaped into useful blades and tools; flint knives also had ritual importance and could be personified [S2]. Their sacrificial use does not make every Tecpatl date a prediction of violence. Tecpatl is a year-bearer [S6], and Sahagún’s 1-Flint account describes trecena-specific ritual attention to Huitzilopochtli and Camaxtli [S1].
cultural_and_historical_context:
Flint blades were cutting tools but also carried profound ritual importance because sacrificial knives could be represented as animate, divine objects. In central Mexican imagery, flint could be given a face and teeth, emphasizing that ritual implements possessed sacred agency rather than being merely inert tools.

Tecpatl is one of the four year-bearer signs.

The trecena Ce Tecpatl (1 Flint) was associated in Sahagún’s account with major ritual attention to Huitzilopochtli and Camaxtli, illustrating how a calendrical sign could organize ceremonial action.
app_safe_description: Tecpatl means “Flint.” Its glyph is a sharpened stone blade, an object with both practical and powerful ritual uses. Flint knives could even be personified in sacred imagery. Tecpatl is also one of the four signs used to name years.

name: Quiahuitl
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Quiahuitl means rain.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: Rain was essential to crops and agricultural timing. It belongs to a sacred geography of mountains, clouds, caves, and springs [S2, S3]. Rain nourishes but storms, hail, and floods can be destructive. Broad rain symbolism should not be conflated with a specific manuscript’s patron assignment.
cultural_and_historical_context:
Rain was one of the most consequential forces in central Mexican life. Agricultural success depended on the timing and amount of rainfall, and the rain-and-mountain complex centered on Tlaloc, the Tlaloque, sacred mountains, caves, springs, and agricultural fertility.

Rain could be sustaining but also destructive—hail, flood, and storm belonged to the same powerful atmospheric world.

A day-sign patron table and the broad religious meaning of rain are not identical. Although Tlaloc is the best-known rain deity, the patron listed for the individual Quiahuitl sign in a particular calendrical scheme may be another deity. The app should cite the specific manuscript tradition used for patron fields.
app_safe_description: Quiahuitl means “Rain.” Rain sustained maize agriculture and tied human communities to mountains, clouds, springs, and powerful rain deities. Its sacred importance came from that double capacity to nourish life and to arrive with dangerous force.

name: Xochitl
literal_meaning_and_glyph: Xochitl means flower and closes the sequence of twenty day signs.
core_meanings_and_symbolism: Flowers evoke beauty, fragrance, and preciousness, and can carry fertility, sexuality, offering, and ritual associations [S2, S7]. “Flower and song” (in xochitl in cuicatl) evokes elevated artistic expression. Durán connects the 1-Flower trecena with artisans; that account is not a universal reading of every Xochitl day [S7].
cultural_and_historical_context:
Flowers were exceptionally rich signs in Nahua culture. They belonged to beauty, fragrance, fertility, sexuality, offerings, song, poetry, preciousness, and artistic creation. The paired expression in xochitl in cuicatl—“flower and song”—became a way of speaking about elevated artistic, poetic, and philosophical expression in Nahua traditions.

Flower imagery is closely connected with deities such as Xochiquetzal and Xochipilli.
app_safe_description: Xochitl means “Flower.” Flowers were symbols of beauty, fertility, fragrance, offerings, artistry, song, and precious expression. In colonial descriptions of the divinatory calendar, the 1-Flower trecena is especially connected with artistic and skilled work.
